introduction-the-language-of-time-series.core: PromQL is a functional query language over labelled time series. Expressions return instant vectors (one value per series at a time), range vectors (a window of samples per series), or scalars. You select series by name and labels, transform range vectors with functions like rate(), aggregate across labels with sum by(), and combine with arithmetic. Grafana renders those queries as dashboards with variables and annotations.

first_principles.problem: Engineers copy queries from blogs without understanding why some return errors like 'expected range vector'.

analogy.title: Spreadsheet formulas over a column of readings
analogy.story: Pick the rows (selectors), compute changes over a period (functions), then total by category (aggregation).
analogy.breaks: Spreadsheets have fixed rows; series appear and vanish with pods.

code.text:
http_requests_total                 # instant vector
http_requests_total[5m]             # range vector
rate(http_requests_total[5m])       # instant vector (per-second rate)
sum(http_requests_total[5m])        # ERROR: sum expects instant vector

check.q: What's the difference between an instant vector and a range vector?
check.a: An instant vector has one sample per series at a point in time; a range vector has all samples per series within a time window.

basic-selectors-finding-the-needle.core: A selector picks series by metric name and label matchers: = equals, != not equals, =~ regex match and !~ regex not match. For example http_requests_total{service="checkout", status=~"5.."}. The metric name is itself the __name__ label. Regexes are fully anchored. Selecting too broadly is slow and expensive, and an empty matcher on a missing label matches series without that label.

first_principles.problem: A query for errors also matches health-check traffic and staging, inflating the error rate.

analogy.title: Filtering a contacts list
analogy.story: 'City = London AND job starts with Eng', not scrolling through everyone.
analogy.breaks: Contacts apps do partial matches; PromQL regexes match the whole value.

code.text:
http_requests_total{env="prod", service="checkout", status=~"5..", route!="/healthz"}
{__name__=~"http_.*_total", job="api"}   # by name pattern

check.q: Does {service=~"api"} match a series with service="api-gateway"?
check.a: No, PromQL regexes are fully anchored; you'd need "api.*".

rate-vs-increase-the-most-common-confusi.core: rate(counter[5m]) gives the per-second average increase over the window, handling counter resets: use it for graphs and alerts. increase(counter[1h]) gives the total increase over the window (rate × seconds), which reads well as 'requests in the last hour'. irate uses only the last two samples, so it's spiky. The range should be at least 4× the scrape interval, and you take rate before aggregating: sum(rate()), never rate(sum()).

first_principles.problem: A dashboard shows huge spikes and drops because it applies rate() after sum(), mangling counter resets.
derivation: Use **increase()** for totals in a window.

analogy.title: Speed vs distance travelled
analogy.story: rate is your average speed over five minutes; increase is how many miles you covered in the hour.
analogy.breaks: Odometers rarely reset; counters reset every deploy.

code.text:
sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))      # ✔ requests/sec per service
sum by (service) (increase(http_requests_total[1h]))  # ✔ requests in last hour
rate(sum(http_requests_total)[5m:])                   # ✘ resets broken by sum

check.q: Why must you apply rate() before sum() and not after?
check.a: rate() detects counter resets per series; summing first merges series so resets look like large drops, corrupting the result.

aggregation-summing-up.core: Aggregation operators (sum, avg, max, min, count, topk, quantile) collapse series across labels. 'by (labels)' keeps only those labels; 'without (labels)' drops the listed ones and keeps the rest. Aggregation is how you go from per-pod series to per-service or per-region views. Choose the labels you keep deliberately, because anything dropped can't be split later in that query.

first_principles.problem: A per-pod latency dashboard has 300 lines and is unreadable.

analogy.title: Rolling up sales by region
analogy.story: From every till receipt to totals per store, then per region.
analogy.breaks: Sales roll-ups are additive; latency percentiles are not.

code.text:
sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
topk(5, sum by (pod) (rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total[5m])))
count by (service) (up == 1)
sum without (pod, instance) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))

check.q: What's the difference between 'sum by (service)' and 'sum without (pod)'?
check.a: by keeps only service; without drops only pod and keeps all other labels.

arithmetic-and-multi-metric-queries.core: Binary operators (+ − * / and comparisons) between vectors match series with identical label sets. When label sets differ you control matching: on(labels) or ignoring(labels) choose the join keys, and group_left or group_right allow many-to-one joins, for example enriching series with labels from an info metric like kube_pod_info. This is how you compute ratios (error rate), utilisation (used ÷ limit) and joins across metrics.

first_principles.problem: An error-rate query returns nothing because the numerator and denominator have different label sets.
derivation: **Aggregate both sides** to the same labels.

analogy.title: A spreadsheet VLOOKUP
analogy.story: Match rows by a key column to combine figures from two tables.
analogy.breaks: VLOOKUP finds one match; PromQL errors on unexpected many-to-many matches.

code.text:
# error ratio: both sides aggregated by service
sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]))
/ sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))

# memory use vs limit, enriched with node label
sum by (pod, namespace) (container_memory_working_set_bytes)
/ on (pod, namespace) group_left(node)
sum by (pod, namespace, node) (kube_pod_container_resource_limits{resource="memory"})

check.q: Why aggregate both sides by the same labels before dividing?
check.a: Binary operators only match series with identical label sets; mismatched labels produce empty results.

histograms-and-quantiles-the-hard-math.core: histogram_quantile(φ, ...) estimates quantiles from cumulative bucket counters. Take rate() of the _bucket series, sum by le (plus any grouping labels; le must be kept), then apply the function, which finds the bucket containing the φ-quantile and interpolates linearly within it. Accuracy depends on bucket edges, results are capped at the highest finite bucket, and averaging quantiles is mathematically wrong.

first_principles.problem: A p99 query shows exactly 10 s constantly because all slow requests fall in the +Inf bucket above 10 s.
truths: Interpolation assumes even spread within a bucket.

analogy.title: Estimating the median height from grouped data
analogy.story: If you know how many people fall in each 10 cm band, you can estimate the median within its band.
analogy.breaks: Height data rarely clusters at one edge; latency often does.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Per-route tail latency across all pods.

code.text:
histogram_quantile(0.95,
  sum by (le, route) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{service="checkout"}[5m])))
# Apdex-style: satisfied (<0.3s) ratio
sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.3"}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count[5m]))

check.q: Why must the le label be kept when summing histogram buckets?
check.a: histogram_quantile needs the bucket boundaries (le) to locate and interpolate the quantile.

grafana-variables-build-once-use-everywh.core: Grafana dashboard variables turn hardcoded values into dropdowns: a query variable like label_values(up, cluster), then namespace dependent on cluster, then service. Panels reference $cluster and $service, so one dashboard serves every service and environment. Multi-value and 'All' options need regex matchers (=~"$service"), and chained variables keep dropdowns relevant.

first_principles.problem: A team maintains 60 nearly identical dashboards, one per service, all slightly out of date.
truths: Dashboards differ mostly by filter values.

analogy.title: A form letter with mail-merge fields
analogy.story: One template, personalised per recipient by filling in fields.
analogy.breaks: Mail merge is offline; variables re-query live data.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: One dashboard for every service and cluster.

code.text:
Variable service: label_values(http_requests_total{cluster="$cluster"}, service)  (multi, include All)

Panel query:
sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total{cluster="$cluster", service=~"$service", status=~"5.."}[$__rate_interval]))
/ sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total{cluster="$cluster", service=~"$service"}[$__rate_interval]))

check.q: Why use =~ instead of = with a multi-value Grafana variable?
check.a: Multiple selections are rendered as a regex alternation (a|b), which requires the regex matcher.

grafana-annotations-correlating-events-w.core: Annotations overlay events (deploys, feature-flag flips, incidents, config changes) as vertical markers on time-series panels. They come from the Grafana API (posted by CI/CD), from queries (Prometheus changes() on version labels, Loki log events), or manual notes. Seeing 'latency jumped right at deploy v2.3.1' turns hours of guessing into seconds.

first_principles.problem: Latency jumped at 14:05, and the team spends an hour discovering a deploy happened at 14:04.
truths: Change events can be recorded automatically.

analogy.title: Sticky notes on a timeline
analogy.story: 'New chef started here' explains why reviews changed that week.
analogy.breaks: Sticky notes are written later; annotations should be automatic.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Every deploy appears as a marker on graphs.

code.text:
curl -s -X POST https://grafana.acme.com/api/annotations \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GRAFANA_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"tags\":[\"deploy\",\"checkout\",\"prod\"],\"text\":\"checkout $VERSION by $GITHUB_ACTOR\"}"

check.q: Why are deploy annotations so valuable during incidents?
check.a: Most incidents follow changes, and seeing a deploy marker aligned with a metric shift points straight to the likely cause.
